---
title: "Design"
---

## Architecture

Two execution paths around one model core, both removing
`MKT → SIZE → HML → MOM`. Research prepares whole arrays at once; live processing
changes one return at a time.

- **Shared:** the prepared exposures, the configured residualizer, the period's
  regression weights, `CrossSectionFit`, and the rule that only a final fit
  advances factor state.
- **Not shared:** input transport, scheduling, provisional-result handling, and
  output containers.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    history["Historical market frames"] --> batch["run_pipeline"]
    batch --> vector["Vectorized universe, returns, factors, and weights"]
    vector --> canonical["SequentialOLSResidualizer.fit"]

    feed["Canonical live events"] --> log["JsonlEventLog"]
    log --> live["LiveRegressionRunner"]
    live --> provisional["IncrementalRegression provisional fits"]
    live --> canonical

    vector --> bridge["historical_events"]
    bridge --> log
    canonical --> final["Final CrossSectionFit"]
    final --> state["PreparedFactorModel.update"]
```

The event bridge lets the same historical returns go through the log as recorded
events. Research keeps the vectorized path, and the replay proves the two agree.

### Research sequence

The batch path vectorizes data preparation, then iterates dates so recursive
state advances in point-in-time order:

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as MarketDataSource
    participant U as UniverseBuilder
    participant P as run_pipeline
    participant M as FactorModel
    participant F as PreparedFactorModel
    participant W as RegressionWeightModel
    participant R as Residualizer
    participant V as Validations
    P->>U: build(source, window)
    U->>S: Load dated market-cap snapshots
    U-->>P: Point-in-time membership
    P->>S: Load member history
    P->>M: prepare(data, returns, universe)
    M-->>P: Prepared model
    P->>W: calculate(data)
    W-->>P: Dated regression weights
    loop Each trading date
        P->>F: exposures(date, tickers)
        F-->>P: Raw exposures
        P->>R: fit(returns, exposures, weights)
        R-->>P: CrossSectionFit
        P->>F: update(date, fit)
    end
    P->>V: validate(result)
    V-->>P: Named validation results
```

`run_pipeline` coordinates the stages and returns an in-memory
`ResidualizationResult`. Writing remains separate.

### Live sequence

The live path records each event before applying it. Tick updates are cheap
revisions. At period close it goes back to the configured residualizer before any
state moves.

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Feed adapter
    participant L as EventLog
    participant P as LiveRegressionRunner
    participant F as PreparedFactorModel
    participant I as IncrementalRegression
    participant R as Residualizer
    participant O as Output sink
    A->>P: capture(PeriodOpened with membership and weights)
    P->>L: append and fsync
    P->>F: exposures(as_of, tickers)
    P->>I: initialize(raw exposures, frozen weights)
    loop ReturnObserved
        A->>P: capture(return revision)
        P->>L: append and fsync
        P->>I: update(ticker, return)
        I-->>P: provisional CrossSectionFit
        P-->>O: revisioned provisional result
    end
    A->>P: capture(PeriodClosed)
    P->>L: append and fsync
    P->>I: finalize()
    I->>R: canonical fit(all returns, exposures, weights)
    R-->>I: final CrossSectionFit
    I-->>P: final CrossSectionFit
    P->>F: update(as_of, final fit)
    P-->>O: final LivePeriodResult
```

Replay substitutes ordered events read from `EventLog` for the feed-adapter
calls. Everything after event delivery is the same.

### Research and live side by side

| Phase | Research | Live | Shared rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | Range-loaded DataFrames | Durable ordered events | Stable ticker IDs, decimal returns, named exposures |
| Period start | Select membership and lagged weights | `PeriodOpened` freezes membership and weights | Inputs use only prior-known state |
| Returns | Whole daily cross-section | `ReturnObserved` revises one ticker | One common return horizon per fit |
| Open-period fit | None | Incremental provisional revisions | Same exposure normalization and model columns |
| Final fit | One canonical fit per date | Canonical reconciliation at `PeriodClosed` | Same residualizer, weights, and fit result |
| State | Update after each historical fit | Update only after final close | Final fit advances `PreparedFactorModel` once |
| Output | `ResidualizationResult`, validations, CSV | Revisioned `LivePeriodResult` | Factor returns, residual returns, diagnostics |
| Recovery | Rerun vectorized history | Restore and replay the event log | Deterministic point-in-time ordering |

The I/O and scheduling layers differ on purpose. Research wants range scans and
vectorized frames. Live operation wants subscriptions, watermarks, revisions,
durability, and recovery. They meet at the prepared exposures and the canonical
residualizer, not behind a shared read API that would suit neither.

## Stage contracts

### Market data

`MarketDataSource` provides:

- `latest_date(end)`: the last available observation on or before an endpoint.
- `trading_dates(start, end)`: sorted observed exchange dates.
- `load(start, end, tickers)`: a DataFrame indexed by normalized
  `(date, ticker)`, with decimal-compatible `return_percent` and numeric
  `market_cap`.

Ticker identifiers must be stable strings. Missing observations are allowed;
later stages drop unusable rows. A different feed only needs an adapter for this
frame and calendar.

### Universe

`UniverseBuilder.build` returns a Boolean Series indexed by
`(date, ticker)`. `DailyTopMarketCapUniverse` ranks all observed names by
the previous trading day's market cap, with ticker as a deterministic tie
breaker, so membership is known before the return it applies to.

### Returns

`ReturnCalculator.calculate` maps canonical market data to a decimal-return
Series named `return`. `PercentageReturns` converts marcap's
corporate-action-aware percentage return field; it does not reconstruct returns
from close prices.

### Factors

`FactorModel` declares its loading-history padding and prepares a
`PreparedFactorModel`. The prepared model must provide named,
ticker-indexed exposures for each date and accept a post-fit `update`.
Static models make `update` a no-op. Stateful models use it, and the pipeline
never sees their state.

To plug in a vendor exposure model, return its point-in-time exposure matrix
through this interface. If the vendor also supplies factor returns or residual
returns, its adapter replaces the residualizer too, since the local regression
would no longer be estimating them.

### Regression weights

`RegressionWeightModel.calculate` maps canonical market data to a positive Series
indexed by `(date, ticker)`. The configured `EqualRegressionWeights` gives every
usable observation the same influence. `SquareRootMarketCapWeights` uses the
square root of market cap shifted one trading session, so date $t$ never uses its
own close. Either scheme replaces the other without changing the universe,
factors, or estimator.

### Residualization

`Residualizer.fit` receives one day's returns, raw exposures, and regression
weights, and returns a `CrossSectionFit`, or `None` if the cross-section can't be
estimated. The configured `SequentialOLSResidualizer` winsorizes every
exposure once, centers and scales it, removes the intercept, then fits each named
exposure against the residual left by the preceding step. `factor_order` must
match the exposure names exactly, so the attribution order is always explicit.

`unscaled_factors` names exposures that are still winsorized and centered but are
not rescaled to unit variance, so their slopes stay in the exposure's own units.
Centering is not optional. It keeps each exposure orthogonal to the intercept; an
uncentered column would leave the market level and that factor fighting over the
same variation. Every `CrossSectionFit` reports the `exposure_centers` and
`exposure_scales` it applied, so a stateful factor can invert the map instead of
guessing at it.

Alternatives behind the same protocol:

- `SequentialWLSResidualizer` with `SquareRootMarketCapWeights` for a
  cap-weighted ordered fit.
- `OLSResidualizer` for a joint multivariate fit.
- Any robust or vendor-supplied estimator, without changing the other stages.

### Validation and output

Validations consume the completed result and return named metrics. The
configured run checks date coverage, finite values, `r = Xf + ε`, and
orthogonality immediately after each ordered factor is removed. It makes no claim
that final ε is jointly orthogonal to every earlier raw exposure. Failed checks
raise `RegressionValidationError`.

`CsvArtifactWriter` writes ε, r, X, and f atomically. Other formats can write
the result DataFrames directly.

ty checks the callable protocols; integration tests cover the DataFrame
schemas.

## Point-in-time construction

Three ways to pick a universe, and why only one is used:

- **End-of-sample selection applied backward** carries survivor and look-ahead
  bias, because future winners, surviving listings, and later IPOs influence
  earlier research.
- **A first-date snapshot held forward** does not look ahead, but goes stale as
  names list, delist, grow, and shrink. Over one year only a modest fraction of
  large-cap membership turns over, so the staleness is bounded and the bias is
  small. Over ten years it compounds: the snapshot progressively describes a
  different set of stocks than the one that existed, and it silently changes which
  names have enough history to carry a long-window exposure such as HML.
- **Daily re-selection from the prior close** is what the model does. Mean one-way
  membership turnover is 0.75% per day, and the usable output spans 1,916 distinct
  tickers instead of one fixed list of 1,000.

All dated memberships are computed before factor history loads, then the union of
required tickers is read in one pass. That is an I/O optimization only. Factors
still see just each day's membership and lagged data, so future membership never
sets a dated exposure.

## Model choices and timing

The daily universe targets 1,000 names using prior-session market cap. That
threshold captures nearly all listed capitalization while leaving out the low-cap
tail most exposed to sparse trading and stale closes. The walkthrough computes the
[coverage at each size](walkthrough.qmd#universe-choice) from the data, so those
figures are not repeated here.

- **MKT:** recursive market-beta exposure. Initial beta uses pre-window asset
  returns against a lagged-cap-weighted market proxy from the first output
  universe. Each period uses the prior beta; only the finalized MKT slope
  updates the exponentially decayed state for the next period. MKT is centered
  but not rescaled, so its slope is a return per unit of beta, not per standardized
  unit.
- **SIZE:** log market cap lagged one trading observation. Larger names get
  higher exposure, so a positive slope means big-minus-small.
- **HML:** negative compounded return over 1,008 observations shifted by 252,
  with 756 required observations. It captures approximately 12–60 month
  reversal: long-term losers have higher exposure. This is a price-based value
  proxy, not accounting book-to-market HML.
- **MOM:** compounded return over 189 observations shifted by 63, with 126
  required observations, approximating the prior 3–12 month trend.
- **Regression:** sequential OLS after 1% cross-sectional exposure
  winsorization and centering, in the explicit order MKT, SIZE, HML, then MOM.
  SIZE, HML, and MOM are also scaled to unit variance. MKT is not, because beta
  already has a meaningful unit. Every usable observation carries equal weight.

`history_business_days` is loading padding, not a promise of an exact number
of KRX observations. The factor builders enforce their own minimum periods.

The intercept is the market-level return. MKT is high-minus-low beta per unit
of beta; SIZE, HML, and MOM are slopes per standardized exposure unit. These are
realized relative premia, so their signs are not constrained to be positive.

### Recursive beta

Beta must be known before the return it explains:

- Pre-window returns bootstrap beta against a lagged-cap-weighted market proxy.
- A name without enough history starts from the explicit 1.0 prior.
- Period $t$ uses the stored beta, estimates MKT, and updates beta only after the
  fit is final. The updated value first applies to period $t+1$.

The regression can transform raw beta to
$x_i = (\operatorname{winsor}(\beta_i) - c) / s$. Before updating state it
converts the fitted slope $f$ back to a per-beta return $g$ and restores the
centered level:

$$
g = \frac{f}{s}, \qquad
y_i = \varepsilon_i + x_i f + c g.
$$

This keeps the recursive state on the same scale as the bootstrap, prior, and
$\pm5$ bounds. In the evaluated model MKT is unscaled, so $s=1$, but centering
still has to be undone.

The bootstrap and update are related but not identical: the bootstrap uses an
observed market proxy, while the recursion uses the fitted cross-sectional MKT
premium. That feedback makes the beta path sensitive to universe and weighting
choices. With `prior_variance=1e-4` and `decay=0.97`, the prior is worth roughly
25 observations and halves about every 23 trading days.

Sequential removal gives earlier factors first claim on shared variation.
Changing the order changes f, ε, and the model version.

## Evidence that residualization worked

A mechanically correct sequential result should:

- reconstruct raw returns,
- be centered by the intercept,
- be orthogonal to each factor at the moment that factor is removed,
- have enough cross-sectional rank and coverage,
- contain finite values.

A later correlated factor can reintroduce a moment against an earlier exposure, so
final-residual correlations are reported as diagnostics instead of counting as a
failed fit.

A *useful* residual-return series needs more: stable coverage and dispersion,
plausible tails, little residual serial structure, and no known look-ahead. See
[walkthrough.qmd](walkthrough.qmd) for the measured results.

## Authoritative and incremental regression

`SequentialOLSResidualizer.fit` is the authoritative calculation in both modes. It
aligns returns, exposures, and positive weights, drops unusable rows, winsorizes,
then centers every column and scales all but MKT using the same moments the
regression uses. For normalized exposure $x_j$ and fixed weight $w_i$, it
applies

$$
e_i^{(0)} = r_i - \frac{\sum_i w_i r_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad
f_j = \frac{\sum_i w_i x_{ij}e_i^{(j-1)}}{\sum_i w_i x_{ij}^2}, \qquad
e_i^{(j)} = e_i^{(j-1)} - x_{ij}f_j
$$

for $j =$ MKT, SIZE, HML, MOM. The final $e^{(4)}$ is ε, and the stored
terms satisfy $r = Xf + \varepsilon$. R² and stage orthogonality use that same
$w$, which is uniform in the configured run. Residual dispersion stays a separate
downstream diagnostic. `OLSResidualizer.fit` does the same job in one joint
`numpy.linalg.lstsq` call, behind the same protocol.

`IncrementalRegression` speeds up either canonical method. It is not a second
model:

- During an open period it holds raw exposures fixed.
- A ticker's first usable return rebuilds through the configured residualizer,
  because the cross-section and normalization changed.
- Once rows are stable, a cached linear coefficient map applies one return delta
  without repeating normalization or all regressions, then recalculates ε. For the
  sequential model that map comes from the same ordered
  residual-on-residual recurrence, so its cost scales with the small factor set
  instead of a dense cross-section matrix.

At `PeriodClosed`, `IncrementalRegression.finalize` reruns the canonical fit from
accumulated returns and raw exposures. Only that result is final, and only it can
advance recursive factor state, so drift in the accelerator never reaches the
model. The parity test runs market-first sequential OLS through
`run_pipeline`, the live event stream, and a reopened log, requiring factor and
residual returns to match within `1e-12`.

## Performance characteristics

With four factors and roughly 840 names per cross-section, data movement,
normalization, and output cost more than the regression. The main constraints
are:

- **Dates must run in order.** Recursive beta for period $t+1$ depends on the
  finalized fit for period $t$, so the date loop cannot be parallelized. Everything
  before it is columnar and vectorized: market reads, returns, static factors,
  universe construction. Independent markets, intervals, or model versions can still
  run on separate workers.
- **Memory grows with output, not with the fit.** The full result accumulates in
  memory, so storage scales with modeled rows times factors. Active model state is
  only one cross-section.
- **Durability sets the live latency floor.** `JsonlEventLog.append` fsyncs before
  processing, which can cost more than the regression. `append_many` amortizes it.
  Exact event replay works one recorded observation at a time and is slower than
  vectorized research by design.

The ten-year OLS run covers 2,451 dates and 2,054,729 rows in roughly two minutes
end to end, peaking near 1.6 GiB. That is one machine, not a guarantee. No intraday
latency claim is made at all, since marcap is daily and there is no real feed
adapter.

## Event log and replay

`JsonlEventLog` is a durable, single-process reference implementation of the
`EventLog` protocol. `LiveRegressionRunner.capture` appends and fsyncs an event
before applying it, so acknowledged model state never leads its recorded input.
`append_many` batches that durability cost. Event IDs are idempotent: appending
the same ID and content returns its existing offset, while conflicting content
is rejected.

The Pydantic event schemas are:

- `PeriodOpened`: `(market, interval, as_of)` plus aligned fixed-period tickers and regression weights.
- `ReturnObserved`: one ticker's latest same-horizon decimal return, with
  `effective_at`, `known_at`, source sequence, and source revision.
- `PeriodClosed`: the watermark decision that makes the current fit final.

The log assigns a contiguous ingestion offset. `LiveRegressionRunner.replay`
consumes those offsets in recorded order. Input events do not contain a model
version, so the same log can be replayed through another model; each
`LivePeriodResult` does contain the required model version.

`historical_events` turns a point-in-time universe and return Series into the same
open/observe/close stream. It is the slow, exact-replay path used for parity checks
and debugging. Normal research keeps the vectorized DataFrame path.

Console logs are not the replay source. Production telemetry can record latency,
coverage, rank, R², model version, and input offset, but the event ledger is the
durable input history.

## Live period semantics

`LiveRegressionRunner` owns one `(market, interval)` at a time:

- **Open** fixes the period membership and prior-state exposures.
- **Observations** revise only the same-horizon return vector.
- **Close** performs the canonical fit and is the only step that advances factor
  state.

Every emitted `LivePeriodResult` carries the model version, period key, input
offset, revision, and final/provisional flag.

Every name in a cross-section needs the same return horizon. An intraday adapter
would translate ticks into previous-close-to-latest or bar-open-to-latest returns.
Irregular ticker-to-ticker returns are not a cross-section.

A first intraday version would:

- freeze membership and slow styles from the prior close;
- publish provisional factor and residual returns on each tick; and
- advance recursive beta only on finalized bars.

An intraday model also needs decay expressed in bars or trading-time half-life,
with a separate model version from the daily fit.

Marcap supplies daily observations, so this repository can prove daily
batch/replay equivalence but cannot demonstrate a real intraday feed.

### Corrections, recovery, and checkpoints

Before close, a later `ReturnObserved` event can revise a ticker and the final fit
naturally includes it. After recursive state has advanced, a correction must not
mutate history in place. Append the correction, restore state from a checkpoint
before the affected period, then replay forward to issue revised outputs.

What exists today versus what production needs:

- **Implemented:** durable capture, replay from the start of a log, and the
  runner's last processed offset.
- **Missing:** serialization of prepared-factor and open-period state. A
  production checkpoint must also carry the model version, active cross-section,
  and last offset.

The event log remains authoritative; checkpoints are disposable acceleration.

### Non-overlapping market hours

This is an information-alignment problem at every frequency. A closed market's
return is missing, not zero.

Use one clock and watermark per market:

- **Overlap:** align both markets to the same UTC interval. Finalize after both
  watermarks; a halt, missing bar, or late observation stays missing.
- **No overlap:** keep separate market-local fits. For KRX, treat the previous US
  session as a lagged opening input, freeze US beta before the local open, and
  remove it before local MKT. If the US factor return is trusted directly, remove
  `US_BETA × US_RETURN` as a fixed component instead.

Treat the overnight gap and regular session as separate horizons; do not reapply
the foreign close to every bar. Require `known_at <= as_of`, reject stale inputs,
and record the session and revision so research replay matches live processing.

## Limitations and extensions

- **Sparse factor set.** No sector, industry, accounting-value, liquidity, or
  volatility data is imported, so that common structure stays in ε.
- **HML costs coverage.** It requires 756 observations inside its long window, so
  the fitted sample averages 838.3 names and bottoms at 795 against a 1,000-name
  target. A shorter proxy or a neutral missing-exposure policy would recover the
  coverage but define a different model.
- **Recursive beta is noisy and path-dependent.** The fitted MKT slope updates
  the next beta, while each name has roughly 1:19 signal to residual-return noise
  in the evaluated run. Dispersion reaches the $\pm5$ bound, and names can
  re-enter with stale state. Shrinkage, slower decay, or an independent market
  proxy would help; the last option would define a different model and give up
  cross-sectional orthogonality to beta.
- **Event and data tails remain.** Marcap's return field handles its source's
  corporate-action adjustments, but the maximum absolute residual is above 100%.
  Downstream studies need their own event filters or robust treatment.
- **The checks are in-sample.** Stage orthogonality and R² are cross-sectional
  identities, not evidence that these factors predict returns.
